angulo_em_uma_frase: A espinha é a divisória continental: uma linha que corre pela cordilheira ocidental dos Andes, a menos de 70 milhas do centro de Lima, e parte a água do Peru. Tudo se mostra em relação a ela: a água e a gente de cada lado (p1), a chuva que muda ao cruzá-la (p2), os vales e o porto que puseram a gente e a capital no lado seco (p3), a descida das montanhas por onde ela passa (p4), o túnel que a atravessa (p5), a borda da cidade aonde o cano não chega (p6) e a passagem única (p7). O mapa é o protagonista nas cenas de lugar; onde a fala não é espacial (a citação, o censo, a reportagem), a linha fica acesa no fundo e não força a cena.

decisoes_da_sala_aplicadas.decisao: Título de trabalho do Lucas (17/10/2026): 'Why Peru Lives on the Dry Side of the Andes'.
decisoes_da_sala_aplicadas.como: As 3 primeiras frases do gancho têm 'Andes' e 'Peru' (S1), o lado amazônico com a água (S2) e 'the dry side' com 'about 2 percent' (S3). espinha: A linha (a divisória continental) e o que ela parte: a água de um lado, a gente do outro. A pergunta do título se responde em camadas, cada uma paga numa parte, e a água que a capital precisa atravessa a linha de volta por um túnel só.
resumo: Uma linha corre pelos Andes e parte a água do Peru: a leste, três quartos do país e mais de 97 % da água; a oeste, o lado seco, com ~2 % e, em 2012, mais de três em cinco peruanos (PNRH). O vídeo mostra a linha e o que ela parte (p1), por que o oeste é seco (p2), por que a gente está lá mesmo assim: os vales e o porto (p3) e a descida das montanhas no século XX (p4); e como a capital resolve a água atravessando a linha por um túnel só (p5), o que a borda da cidade vive (p6) e o que é depender de uma passagem só (p7), até a resposta e a coda que devolve o título.
pergunta: Why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of the Andes?
pergunta_no_gancho: So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line?
pergunta_longa: Se do outro lado da linha estão três quartos do país e mais de 97 % da água, por que a maioria dos peruanos (mais de três em cinco em 2012) e a capital estão no lado seco, e como a capital vive ali?

tese.frase: O Peru não mora no lado seco por causa da água, e sim por camadas: os vales que os rios curtos abrem no deserto (cidade há uns 5.000 anos), a capital espanhola posta em 1535 junto a um porto muito bom ('partly because') e a descida das montanhas no século XX, que fez da costa a maior região e de Lima e Callao um terço do país. A água teve de ser levada a eles: por canal nos vales antigos, por um túnel através dos Andes desde o começo dos anos 1960 (mais da metade da reserva da estiagem de Lima fica do outro lado da linha) e, na borda da cidade, por caminhão.
o_que_ela_nao_diz: Não diz que 'dois terços' moram hoje no lado seco: o número com ano é 62,53 % (2012); nunca 'two in three', 'two-thirds', 'today' nem 'count' (tr-01, R01).

Não diz que a maioria dos peruanos mora no deserto: o deserto do MINAM é ecossistema e exclui cidades e lavouras; a Costa do INEI é corte por distrito; o lado seco é corte por bacia (R03, R12, tr-15).
Não diz que o lado seco é seco de cima a baixo: as encostas altas do lado do Pacífico chovem no verão; 'dry' mede a parte da água (~2 %) e a costa de deserto (R40).
Não diz que a montanha sozinha faz o deserto: para o SENAMHI, a causa principal é o ar que desce; a cordilheira 'contribuye' (R14, mec.div-07).
Não diz que nunca chove em Lima: há garoa, e chuva forte em anos de El Niño (o portão reprova 'never rains').
Não diz que a costa sempre foi o centro do Peru: em 1940, 65 % moravam na Sierra (p4; R13).
Não diz que Lima bebe uma fração da sua água pelo túnel: o que se paga é a parte da RESERVA da estiagem (157 de 282, 2007); nenhuma fração do consumo (tr-05, tr-06, R07, R25).
Não diz que toda a água de Lima passa pelo túnel: o 'único medio' é para a água guardada do lado do Atlântico; a cidade capta também o Rímac natural, o Chillón, o Lurín e poços (R06, lim.afi-01).
Não diz que o túnel foi feito só para a luz: o SENAMHI dá também 'afianzar el caudal de río Rímac' (R09).
Não diz que o túnel de Lima é o único a cruzar a linha (Olmos, R20).
Não diz quando o segundo túnel sai: em 2026, sem data de obra (R10).
Não aponta vilão: nem a SEDAPAL, nem a Defensoría, nem a mina Ariana (fora do roteiro).
Não dá a população de hoje do lado seco: ninguém a calculou com o censo de 2017 ou de 2025 (doc.lac-01).

promessa: O gancho promete: (1) mostrar a linha e o que ela parte (a água de um lado, a gente do outro); (2) explicar por que o lado oeste é o seco; (3) explicar por que, mesmo assim, mais de três em cinco peruanos moravam ali em 2012; (4) mostrar como a capital, num litoral de deserto, guarda mais da metade da água da estiagem do outro lado da linha e a passa por um túnel só, do começo dos anos 1960. A pergunta: por que a maioria dos peruanos mora no lado seco da linha?

payoff.resposta: As camadas (os vales, o porto, a gente que desceu), já pagas em p3 e p4, e a água levada a elas, paga em p3, p5 e p6. Nenhum número novo na resposta.
payoff.texto_previsto_em_ingles: So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line? Not because that side has the water. First, the valleys: about 5,000 years ago, people built a city above one of them. Then the port: in 1535, the Spanish put their capital near a very good one. Then the people: in the 20th century, the country came down from the mountains, to the coast and to that capital. The water had to be brought to them: by canal in the old valleys, through a tunnel across the Andes since the early 1960s, and at the city's edge, by truck.
payoff.onde: p7, o 3º parágrafo, seguido da coda (o 4º), sobre a qual entra a pergunta do comentário.

gancho.texto:
A line runs along the Andes and divides Peru. East of it, about three-quarters of the country drains toward the Amazon and holds more than 97 percent of Peru's water. West of it, toward the Pacific, is the dry side, with about 2 percent. But that is where most Peruvians live. In 2012, by the national water plan's figures, more than three in five did.

The coast on that side is mostly desert. There, the capital, Lima, gets about a third of an inch of rain a year. With its port, Callao, it is home to more than ten million people. And more than half of the water Lima stores for the dry season sits in lakes on the other side of the line. That water reaches the city through a single tunnel, built in the early 1960s. So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line? You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of Peru's water divide begins.
gancho.paga_o_titulo_nas_3_primeiras_frases: S1 'A line runs along the Andes and divides Peru.' ('Peru' e 'Andes', o que o portão exige); S2 o lado amazônico com 'more than 97 percent of Peru's water'; S3 'West of it, toward the Pacific, is the dry side, with about 2 percent.' (o 'Dry Side' do título, com o '2 percent' e o lado nomeado). O 'Lives' do título é S4, depois de 44 palavras: 'But that is where most Peruvians live.'

tempos.tempo: a escala com a comparação: a linha e os dois lados
tempos.texto: A line runs along the Andes and divides Peru. East of it, about three-quarters of the country drains toward the Amazon and holds more than 97 percent of Peru's water. West of it, toward the Pacific, is the dry side, with about 2 percent.
tempos.cuidado: Uma fonte só, o PNRH (tr-02). 'Divides Peru', nunca 'splits Peru in two': há o terceiro pedaço, o Titicaca, que p1 nomeia. 'Of Peru's water', nunca 'of the rain' (R02). 'About 2 percent' cobre todas as fontes; o PNRH dá 1,76 % (R40). Nenhum decimal na voz do gancho: o portão parte frase em ponto, e '97.9' viraria duas frases.

tempos.tempo: o 'But': a gente está do lado seco
tempos.texto: But that is where most Peruvians live. In 2012, by the national water plan's figures, more than three in five did.
tempos.cuidado: É a contradição do título. 'Most' no presente vale pelos 62,53 % de 2012 e pela Costa do censo de 2025 (58,7 %), toda no lado do Pacífico; a tela mostra só o PNRH com o ano ('62.5% OF THE PEOPLE (2012)'). A forma da S5 é a da R01 ('by the national water plan's figures'), do plano 'a gente'. Nunca 'two in three', 'two-thirds', 'count', 'today'.

tempos.tempo: o contraste que o mapa mostra: deserto, Lima, a gente
tempos.texto: The coast on that side is mostly desert. There, the capital, Lima, gets about a third of an inch of rain a year. With its port, Callao, it is home to more than ten million people.
tempos.cuidado: 'The coast on that side is mostly desert' é área (R03: ~65 % da área natural da região costeira, MINAM 2019, conta do canal), nunca a gente morando no deserto; 'on that side' amarra a costa ao lado seco (no lugar do 'Its coast' da linha). A chuva é a normal do SENAMHI (8 mm ≈ 0,31 pol.), nunca os 10 mm da SEDAPAL nem os 0,4 mm da Mongabay. 'More than ten million' são Lima e Callao censados em 2025 (10.643.581); o 'about a third' do país só em p4, para não colar no 'a third of an inch' (tr-10).

tempos.tempo: a segunda virada, que vira a pergunta: a água da capital está do outro lado
tempos.texto: And more than half of the water Lima stores for the dry season sits in lakes on the other side of the line. That water reaches the city through a single tunnel, built in the early 1960s. So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line?
tempos.cuidado: S9 é a frase da Sala e da R07 ('on the other side of the line'). S10: 'single tunnel' é a palavra da SEDAPAL e da Defensoría; o sujeito é 'that water', a guardada, nunca toda a água de Lima (R06); 'built in the early 1960s' cobre 1958–1962 (R08); nunca 'bored' nem 'under the Andes' (R39). A hidrelétrica fica para p5. S11 é a pergunta do título com a linha (R41: nunca 'an Amazon country').

tempos.texto: You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of Peru's water divide begins.
tempos.cuidado: 'Peru's water divide' (do plano 'a água'): o tema em três palavras, que não repete o título e nomeia a linha pelo que ela parte. Uma vez, no fim do gancho, a ≤170 palavras (voz §1, o portão).

beats: b1 · A linha definida, com o terceiro pedaço (nunca 'em dois'): 'That line is the continental divide. Rain that falls on its western side drains to the Pacific. Rain on its eastern side runs into rivers that reach the Amazon, and then the Atlantic. A smaller third region, in the south, drains into Lake Titicaca.' (doc.afi-24: 159 unidades, 62 no Pacífico, 84 no Atlântico, 13 no Titicaca; doc.num-02, doc.num-04, doc-03.) O dono genérico da linha ('Geographers call') saiu: a frase afirma o nome, que é termo comum.

b2 · Onde ela passa: 'In Peru, the divide runs along the western range of the Andes, through the Lima region itself. From downtown Lima, it is less than 70 miles away.' (mec.afi-19; mec.num-55; R44: 'less than 70 miles' é limite, porque a reta de 66,9 mi de Campo de Marte à estação de Marcapomacocha a cruza; a distância mínima não foi medida, doc.lac-06.) Na tela, 'LESS THAN 70 MI' sobre essa reta. Nenhuma geleira na voz nem na tela: o '2 %' das geleiras da INAIGEM colidiria com o ~2 % da água (tr-10), e o degelo do Rímac não foi medido (mec.lac-03).

b3 · Os rios e o vazio do lado da água: 'On the dry side, dozens of short, steep rivers drop from the mountains to the sea. Lima's own river, the Rímac, is one of them. On the other side, the rivers are long, and they gather into the Amazon. There, Loreto, Peru's largest department, is also one of its least populated. Its capital, Iquitos, can only be reached by air or river, as Harvard's Growth Lab puts it.' (mec.afi-13; doc.num-40 só na tela, 'RÍMAC · ABOUT 90 MI LONG · ANA': na voz, o mesmo '90 miles' de Caral em p3 teria outro sentido, tr-10; gen.afi-26; gen.afi-25 com a correção do laudo: o HKS diz só 'can only be reached by air or river'; nunca 'the largest city in the world without road access'. Do plano 'a água'.)

b4 · A régua do PNRH, a mesma do gancho: 'Peru's national water plan sets the two sides side by side. The dry side covers less than a quarter of the country. Per person, the Amazon side has about a hundred times as much water. Peru's own water authority calls that a paradox.' (doc.num-02, doc.afi-02; doc.num-11 e doc.num-25: 189.167 ÷ 1.816 m³ por pessoa ≈ 104×; doc.afi-05, doc-01: o 'paradójicamente' é da ANA de 2009. O 65 % e o 80,4 % da mesma frase nunca na voz nem na tela: R01 e a decisão da Sala sobre o PIB.)

b5 · A ponte: 'Peru's weather service says the main reason the coast is so dry lies out over the Pacific.' (mec.afi-01, mec-01; R14: a causa principal no mar, sem negar a montanha; o 'not in the mountains' da linha saiu.)
partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: A linha é a divisória continental e passa a menos de 70 milhas de Lima. De um lado, rios curtos e pouca água; do outro, rios longos, quase toda a água e um território quase vazio. O próprio governo chama isso de paradoxo.
partes.mapa: MAPA, o protagonista (identidade §1 e §5): o Peru inteiro sobre satélite escurecido, com a divisória acesa como linha contínua de norte a sul (geometria: unidades hidrográficas da ANA ou HydroBASINS, com a licença lida pelo pesquisa-geo: mec.lac-02, doc.lac-08); o lado seco em --destaque, o amazônico em --contraparte, a bacia do Titicaca neutra e rotulada. Zoom no departamento de Lima, com a reta de Campo de Marte à estação de Marcapomacocha cruzando a linha ('LESS THAN 70 MI'). Os rios: a rede curta e quase paralela do lado seco contra a longa e convergente do outro, o Rímac aceso da linha ao mar; Loreto como polígono, Iquitos como ponto. Crédito '© MapTiler © OpenStreetMap contributors' na tela se a base for a MapTiler (o gasto do vídeo 4 não está liberado: riscos).
partes.ilustracao: Duas animações no traço de engenheiro, com a física do ilustrador (identidade §5, 'Animação para explicar' e 'Mais ilustração'; em Opus): (a) a gota na crista: o corte da cordilheira; uma gota cai na crista e se divide, a de oeste desce curta e íngreme ao mar, a de leste faz o caminho longo até o Amazonas; é a imagem que o espectador leva para o resto do vídeo. (b) A água por pessoa: dois bonecos de linha, um em cada lado, cada um com um cubo de água; o do lado amazônico com ~104 vezes o volume (aresta ~4,7×), cota em Inter 84 px ('números e escala').

'The dry side' sempre na voz; 'the Pacific side' só na tela e na saída do túnel (p5).

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
That line is the continental divide. Rain that falls on its western side drains to the Pacific. Rain on its eastern side runs into rivers that reach the Amazon, and then the Atlantic. A smaller third region, in the south, drains into Lake Titicaca.

In Peru, the divide runs along the western range of the Andes, through the Lima region itself. From downtown Lima, it is less than 70 miles away.

On the dry side, dozens of short, steep rivers drop from the mountains to the sea. Lima's own river, the Rímac, is one of them. On the other side, the rivers are long, and they gather into the Amazon. There, Loreto, Peru's largest department, is also one of its least populated. Its capital, Iquitos, can only be reached by air or river, as Harvard's Growth Lab puts it.

Peru's national water plan sets the two sides side by side. The dry side covers less than a quarter of the country. Per person, the Amazon side has about a hundred times as much water. Peru's own water authority calls that a paradox.

Peru's weather service says the main reason the coast is so dry lies out over the Pacific.

partes.titulo: Why the dry side is dry
partes.funcao: demonstrar: o porquê físico, na ordem do SENAMHI (o ar que desce, o mar frio, a tampa), com a montanha ajudando; a prova pelo El Niño; a chuva que o lado seco tem, no alto e no verão
partes.periodo: clima (normais de 1981–2010 e 1991–2020; a ANA de 2009; o MINAM de 2019)
partes.abre_com: a câmera sai do Peru para o oceano, até o 'H' da alta do Pacífico Sul
partes.ponte_entrada: Over the South Pacific sits a vast high-pressure system, and under it, the air sinks.
beats: b1 · O mecanismo: 'Over the South Pacific sits a vast high-pressure system, and under it, the air sinks. Peru's weather service calls that sinking air the main cause of the dry coast. Off the shore, the cold Humboldt Current, cold water rising from the deep and a blanket of low cloud keep the sea unusually cold for its latitude. A lid of warmer air traps the moisture near the ground. It stays as fog, low cloud and drizzle, not rain.' (mec.afi-01; mec.afi-02 com a correção do laudo: as três coisas juntas do SENAMHI mantêm a TSM 'anómalamente baja, en relación a su media latitudinal'; mec.afi-03; mec.afi-04; mec-01, mec-20; R14. Sem a altura da tampa na voz.)

b2 · A prova pelo avesso (do plano 'a água'): 'You can see the system by what happens when it weakens. In El Niño years, the high pressure and the trade winds ease, the cold water stops rising, the sea warms, and the desert coast gets heavy rain and floods.' (mec.afi-22; passado genérico, sem ano nem previsão: o alerta do ENFEN de 2026–27 fica fora, R19.)

b3 · Lima: 'In a normal year, Lima gets about a third of an inch of rain, almost all of it drizzle. The same weather service calls Lima one of the largest cities in the world located in a desert.' b4 · A montanha ajuda: 'The mountains help. They block moist air from the Amazon up to about 16,000 feet. On the eastern slopes, that air rises and falls as rain. partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: O lado seco é seco sobretudo pelo céu e pelo mar: o ar desce, o mar é frio, e uma tampa prende a umidade embaixo; quando o sistema enfraquece (El Niño), chove. A montanha ajuda, segurando o ar úmido do outro lado. A chuva do lado seco cai no alto, no verão, e corre rápido de volta ao mar.
partes.mapa: A câmera sai do Peru para o oceano (identidade §1: a câmera anda, o mapa não corta para outro mapa): o 'H' do SOUTH PACIFIC HIGH e as setas da corrente de Humboldt (traçado esquemático, declarado). beats: b1 · Caral: 'It is called Caral, and it sits on a desert terrace above the green valley of the Supe River, about 90 miles north of Lima. UNESCO calls it the oldest center of civilization in the Americas.' In the Moche Valley, on the north coast, canals made the dry land farmable over the centuries. There stands Chan Chan, the Chimú capital, which UNESCO calls the largest earthen city of the Americas before Columbus. A canal about 50 miles long once supplied it.' (gen.afi-07, gen-15: Lasaponara e Masini, NÃO a UNESCO; R54; a datação é contestada, por isso 'commonly attributed'; o '36 em uso' de Lancho Rojas, 2009, citado, nunca na voz. 'To this day' é presente sem data: o verificador decide se fica, ou a frase sai.)

Their town council's record cites the cold, the snow and the long road to the coast.' Opcional, 2º corte: 'It also says many of the Indigenous people forced to carry their supplies had died doing it.' His order also says the place lay in the middle of the land, where the Indigenous people could serve the Spanish with little work.' (gen.afi-11 e a ressalva do laudo: o 'comedio de tierra' e o 'puedan servir con poco trabajo' tornam o 'partly because' honesto, do plano 'a gente'; R15, R27, R52; 'January 1535' sem o dia: a ordem é de 06/01, em Pachacamac.)

Depois Jauja (ponto: falta a coordenada, Natural Earth/OSM) e a seta Jauja → Lima, com o Callao como porto. Na frase da fundação, a câmera parada e lenta sobre a foz do Rímac, sem rótulo no canto de baixo (o respiro da inscrição: cta.md §5).
partes.ilustracao: Pouca: o mapa e o documento explicam. Se o regente quiser uma, a sequência dos autos em três etapas, montada passo a passo com a voz ('sequências e linhas do tempo'): o pedido do cabildo de Jauja (28/11/1534), a ordem de Pizarro em Pachacamac (06/01/1535), a fundação (janeiro de 1535). Nada de Pizarro desenhado: pessoa real não ganha rosto inventado.
partes.imagens_de_arquivo: A transcrição de Bernabé Cobo (1639; ed. de 1882; gen-19), de domínio público, como DOCUMENTO sobre a mesa, com 'muy buen puerto' grifado em --destaque e a tradução na tela ('BERNABÉ COBO, 1639 (1882 ED.)'); a página sai da mesa antes da frase da fundação (a inscrição). partes.funcao: virar: em 1940 o Peru morava nas montanhas; a descida do século XX, com as causas atribuídas, e a cidade que ela fez
partes.abre_com: o mapa das regiões do censo de 1940, com a Sierra cheia e a Costa rala
partes.ponte_entrada: In 1940, Peru's census found most of them in the highlands, in the mountains the line runs along.
beats: b1 · A virada: 'In 1940, Peru's census found most of them in the highlands, in the mountains the line runs along. Fewer than three in ten lived in the region the census calls the coast.' (doc.num-27: Sierra 65,0 %, Costa 28,3 %; doc-14, doc-10; R12, tr-15: a régua do censo dita na 1ª vez.)

b2 · Censo a censo: 'Then, census by census, the balance tipped.' [o ponto da inscrição de reserva] 'The coast became the largest of the three regions between the censuses of 1961 and 1972. By the 1993 census, more than half of Peruvians lived there. By 2025, nearly six in ten did. Some went east instead, into the rainforest, whose share of Peruvians more than doubled.' 'Peru's statistics institute put it this way: the population had gone from "predominantly Andean" to "mostly coastal."' (doc.num-27: Costa 39,0 → 46,1 contra Sierra 52,3 → 44,0; 52,4 em 1993; 58,7 em 2025; Selva 6,7 → 14,6; doc.afi-09; gen.afi-27; doc.afi-10; R13, evt.D12: nunca 'most Peruvians lived on the coast by 1972'. A selva, do plano 'a gente': a descida não foi só para a costa.)

b3 · As causas, atribuídas: 'In a 1995 study, the same institute pointed to a shortage of farmland in the highlands, and called the coast the main destination of people leaving the Andes. Later, the violence of the 1980s and '90s pushed many more. Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission estimated that about half a million people were displaced, many of them to Lima.' (gen.afi-16, gen.afi-17, do plano 'a gente'; gen.afi-21, gen.num-20, gen-08; R43: nunca 'poverty' atribuída ao INEI; R18; nunca 'terrorist' na voz.)

b4 · A capital: 'Lima and Callao grew from about 650,000 people in 1940 to more than ten and a half million in 2025, from about one in ten Peruvians to about a third.' (gen.num-10: 645.172; gen.num-11: 10,4 %; doc.num-33, doc.afi-11: 10.643.581, 32,5 %; R11, tr-03: a soma declarada na tela.) Opcional, 1º corte: 'In 2022, Lima and Callao alone produced about two-fifths of Peru's economic output, by the statistics institute's estimate.' (doc.num-38, doc.afi-17; R22.)

b5 · A cidade que a descida fez: 'Many newcomers built their own homes at the city's edge. In May 1971, 180 families who had taken over a plot of land were moved by the government to a vast, semi-desert stretch of sand south of the city. That ground became Villa El Salvador.' (gen.afi-19, gen.num-19, gen-17: 'extenso arenal semi-desértico'; Pamplona de 1971, nunca Pamplona Alta; os '50 km' do autor fora.) 'By 1981, about one in four people in Lima lived in informal settlements, which Peruvians call barriadas, by census figures Peru's truth commission cites.' (gen.num-14, gen-07; R16, tr-04: só 1981 fecha; a linha conferida no arquivo local pelo verificador antes da tela.)
b6 · A ponte: 'A city that size needs water all year, and its river runs low for seven months of it.' (lim.num-15, lim.afi-07: maio a novembro.)
partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Em 1940, o Peru morava nas montanhas. No século XX, censo a censo, ele desceu: a costa virou a maior região e passou da metade; a capital foi de um em dez a um terço do país e cresceu sobre a areia. As causas têm dono: a terra que faltava na serra e, depois, a violência.
partes.mapa: As regiões naturais do INEI por distrito (Costa, Sierra, Selva), de 1940 a 2025, com a régua na tela ('THE COAST, AS PERU’S CENSUS DRAWS IT'; geometria: os distritos do INEI com a região natural, pesquisa-geo, doc.lac-08). A linha continua acesa, mas a mancha da Costa do INEI NÃO é o lado seco: rótulo e cor próprios (tr-15). Depois Lima e Callao com Villa El Salvador ao sul (OSM, com o crédito). Setas da serra para a costa só como esquema declarado (direção, não fluxo medido).

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
In 1940, Peru's census found most of them in the highlands, in the mountains the line runs along. Fewer than three in ten lived in the region the census calls the coast.

Then, census by census, the balance tipped. The coast became the largest of the three regions between the censuses of 1961 and 1972. By the 1993 census, more than half of Peruvians lived there. By 2025, nearly six in ten did. Some went east instead, into the rainforest, whose share of Peruvians more than doubled. Peru's statistics institute put it this way: the population had gone from "predominantly Andean" to "mostly coastal."

In a 1995 study, the same institute pointed to a shortage of farmland in the highlands, and called the coast the main destination of people leaving the Andes. Later, the violence of the 1980s and '90s pushed many more. Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission estimated that about half a million people were displaced, many of them to Lima.

Lima and Callao grew from about 650,000 people in 1940 to more than ten and a half million in 2025, from about one in ten Peruvians to about a third. In 2022, Lima and Callao alone produced about two-fifths of Peru's economic output, by the statistics institute's estimate.

Many newcomers built their own homes at the city's edge. In May 1971, 180 families who had taken over a plot of land were moved by the government to a vast, semi-desert stretch of sand south of the city. That ground became Villa El Salvador. By 1981, about one in four people in Lima lived in informal settlements, which Peruvians call barriadas, by census figures Peru's truth commission cites.

A city that size needs water all year, and its river runs low for seven months of it.

b3 · A resposta, em camadas já pagas, sem número novo: 'So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line? Not because that side has the water. First, the valleys: about 5,000 years ago, people built a city above one of them. Then the port: in 1535, the Spanish put their capital near a very good one. Then the people: in the 20th century, the country came down from the mountains, to the coast and to that capital. The water had to be brought to them: by canal in the old valleys, through a tunnel across the Andes since the early 1960s, and at the city's edge, by truck.' (a pergunta é a do gancho, palavra por palavra; 'Not because that side has the water' no lugar do 'Not for the water' da linha; 'the country came down from the mountains' no lugar de 'millions came down'; o tríptico da água, do plano 'a gente'. Peru lives on the dry side of the Andes. From May to November, part of its capital's water comes from the other one.' partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
The water Lima keeps on the far side of those mountains has only one way through. In 2025, Peru's ombudsman, citing the utility's own plan, warned that depending on a single tunnel is a risk in a major earthquake. Lima has been planning a second tunnel since the 1990s. In 2026, it still had no construction date.

Lima's tunnel isn't the only one. In the north, a tunnel about 12 miles long carries water from the Amazon side to farmland on the coast.

So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line? Not because that side has the water. First, the valleys: about 5,000 years ago, people built a city above one of them. Then the port: in 1535, the Spanish put their capital near a very good one. Then the people: in the 20th century, the country came down from the mountains, to the coast and to that capital. The water had to be brought to them: by canal in the old valleys, through a tunnel across the Andes since the early 1960s, and at the city's edge, by truck.

Every May 1, the utility starts letting out its high lakes, and the water on the Amazon side crosses the divide toward the Rímac. Peru lives on the dry side of the Andes. From May to November, part of its capital's water comes from the other one.

cadeia_referencial.regra: Cada referente que volta é chamado do mesmo jeito do começo ao fim; a primeira menção define, e as seguintes não trocam de nome. 'The line' é a espinha, mas não cacoete: no máximo uma vez por parágrafo fora do gancho.
cadeia_referencial.the line: 1ª: 'A line runs along the Andes and divides Peru' (gancho S1); definida em p1: 'That line is the continental divide.' Depois, 'the line' na fala comum e 'the divide' só em frase técnica ('to cross the divide', 'crosses the divide toward the Rímac'). Nunca 'the border', 'the wall', 'the ridge', nem 'splits Peru in two'.
cadeia_referencial.the dry side: 1ª: 'West of it, toward the Pacific, is the dry side' (gancho S3). Depois, sempre 'the dry side' na voz. 'The Pacific side' só na tela e numa frase física (a saída do túnel, p5; 'the wetter part of the Pacific side', p2). Nunca 'the desert side'.
cadeia_referencial.the Amazon side: 1ª: 'East of it, about three-quarters of the country drains toward the Amazon' (gancho S2); 'the Amazon side' a partir de p1. Do ponto de vista de Lima, 'the other side of the line' (gancho S9, p5) e 'the far side of those mountains' (p7). Nunca 'the wet side' nem o departamento de Amazonas.
cadeia_referencial.the coast: 'The coast on that side is mostly desert' (gancho S6, a régua do MINAM); 'the coast' em p1–p3. Em p4, a régua do censo dita na 1ª vez: 'the region the census calls the coast'. As duas réguas nunca no mesmo número (tr-15).
cadeia_referencial.the tunnel: 1ª: 'a single tunnel, built in the early 1960s' (gancho S10); depois 'the tunnel'; 'a single tunnel' de novo no risco (p7). O projeto é 'a second tunnel'; o de Olmos, 'a tunnel about 12 miles long' 'in the north'. Nunca 'secret', 'forgotten', 'hidden', 'trans-Andean'.
cadeia_referencial.the lakes: 'lakes' (gancho S9) e 'lakes and reservoirs high in the Andes' (p5); 'those far-side lakes'; na coda, 'its high lakes'. Nunca 'lagoons'. Marcapomacocha só como a estação.
cadeia_referencial.the stored water: 'the water Lima stores for the dry season' (gancho, p5: a mesma forma, a cifra da memória); 'that water', 'that stored water'; em p7, 'the water Lima keeps on the far side of those mountains'.
cadeia_referencial.Lima: 'the capital, Lima' (gancho S7); 'With its port, Callao' (gancho S8), depois 'Lima and Callao'. 'The city' quando o sujeito é a cidade física. Nunca 'Lima Metropolitana' na voz.
cadeia_referencial.the Rímac: 'Lima's own river, the Rímac' (p1); depois 'the Rímac'; 'the river Lima drinks from' só dentro da frase do SENAMHI (R09).
cadeia_referencial.the highlands: 'the highlands, in the mountains the line runs along' (p4, 1ª vez); depois 'the highlands', 'the mountains' ou 'the Andes'. Nunca 'the Sierra' na voz.
cadeia_referencial.os órgãos: 'Peru's national water plan' (PNRH: gancho, p1); 'Peru's own water authority' / 'Peru's water authority' (a ANA de 2009: p1, p2); 'Peru's weather service' (SENAMHI); 'Peru's census' e 'Peru's statistics institute' (INEI); 'Lima's water utility', depois 'the utility' (SEDAPAL: a 1ª vez em p5 b2); 'Peru's ombudsman' (Defensoría: p5 b1 e p7); 'Peru's water regulator' (Sunass); 'Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission', depois 'Peru's truth commission' (CVR); 'UNESCO'; 'Harvard's Growth Lab'; 'AFP'; 'a German magazine' (KULTURAUSTAUSCH, o nome na tela). Nenhuma sigla na voz, menos UNESCO e AFP.

notas_para_o_roteirista: As frases entre aspas nos beats são o esqueleto medido (esqueleto_medido): passam no portão juntas, e cada uma é o teto do que o beat pode afirmar. O roteirista pode reescrever a forma, nunca afirmar mais que a frase do beat e a evidência dela.
O esqueleto tem 1974 palavras; o orçamento, 2.036. A diferença sai do 'crescer' de p5 (≈ +35) e, se preciso, de p1 e p4; p3 já está acima e é a primeira a ceder. Nada de enchimento.

Cada parte abre por um parágrafo novo; a frase da fundação (p3) fica sozinha num parágrafo (a pausa da inscrição). A coda (p7) tem três frases, sem número.
Passar o gate.mjs a cada troca; a média por frase hoje é 15,9 (teto 18) e a maior frase 31 (teto 34): frase nova acima de 25 palavras pede razão.

esqueleto_medido.texto:
A line runs along the Andes and divides Peru. East of it, about three-quarters of the country drains toward the Amazon and holds more than 97 percent of Peru's water. West of it, toward the Pacific, is the dry side, with about 2 percent. But that is where most Peruvians live. In 2012, by the national water plan's figures, more than three in five did.

The coast on that side is mostly desert. There, the capital, Lima, gets about a third of an inch of rain a year. With its port, Callao, it is home to more than ten million people. And more than half of the water Lima stores for the dry season sits in lakes on the other side of the line. That water reaches the city through a single tunnel, built in the early 1960s. So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line? You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of Peru's water divide begins.

That line is the continental divide. Rain that falls on its western side drains to the Pacific. Rain on its eastern side runs into rivers that reach the Amazon, and then the Atlantic. A smaller third region, in the south, drains into Lake Titicaca.

In Peru, the divide runs along the western range of the Andes, through the Lima region itself. From downtown Lima, it is less than 70 miles away.

On the dry side, dozens of short, steep rivers drop from the mountains to the sea. Lima's own river, the Rímac, is one of them. On the other side, the rivers are long, and they gather into the Amazon. There, Loreto, Peru's largest department, is also one of its least populated. Its capital, Iquitos, can only be reached by air or river, as Harvard's Growth Lab puts it.

Peru's national water plan sets the two sides side by side. The dry side covers less than a quarter of the country. Per person, the Amazon side has about a hundred times as much water. Peru's own water authority calls that a paradox.

Peru's weather service says the main reason the coast is so dry lies out over the Pacific.

Over the South Pacific sits a vast high-pressure system, and under it, the air sinks. Peru's weather service calls that sinking air the main cause of the dry coast. Off the shore, the cold Humboldt Current, cold water rising from the deep and a blanket of low cloud keep the sea unusually cold for its latitude. A lid of warmer air traps the moisture near the ground. It stays as fog, low cloud and drizzle, not rain.

You can see the system by what happens when it weakens. In El Niño years, the high pressure and the trade winds ease, the cold water stops rising, the sea warms, and the desert coast gets heavy rain and floods.

In a normal year, Lima gets about a third of an inch of rain, almost all of it drizzle. The same weather service calls Lima one of the largest cities in the world located in a desert.

The mountains help. They block moist air from the Amazon up to about 16,000 feet. On the eastern slopes, that air rises and falls as rain. East of the Andes, the town of Satipo gets more than six feet of rain a year.

The dry side gets real rain too, but only high up, from December to March. That summer rain runs off fast, down short rivers. In 2009, Peru's water authority said that about half of the flood water from the wetter part of the Pacific side runs back into the sea unused, for lack of storage. Some of these rivers run dry for part of the year.

Along the shore lies a coastal desert of about 27,000 square miles, from Piura in the north to Tacna, at the border with Chile.

And yet people built a city on that coast about 5,000 years ago.

It is called Caral, and it sits on a desert terrace above the green valley of the Supe River, about 90 miles north of Lima. UNESCO calls it the oldest center of civilization in the Americas.

Rivers like the Supe come down from the mountains near the line, and each one leaves a strip of green across the desert. In the Moche Valley, on the north coast, canals made the dry land farmable over the centuries. There stands Chan Chan, the Chimú capital, which UNESCO calls the largest earthen city of the Americas before Columbus. A canal about 50 miles long once supplied it. In the south, near Nazca, underground channels called puquios, commonly attributed to the Nazca culture, carry water to some fields to this day, researchers report.

In late 1534, Pizarro and the Spanish settlers at Jauja, high in the Andes, agreed to move toward the sea. Their town council's record cites the cold, the snow and the long road to the coast. It also says many of the Indigenous people forced to carry their supplies had died doing it.

In January 1535, Pizarro chose a site partly because it had a very good port nearby. His order also says the place lay in the middle of the land, where the Indigenous people could serve the Spanish with little work.

Lima was founded that month, in the Rímac Valley, near the sea and the port of Callao.

Until the mid-1700s, UNESCO says, it was the capital and the most important city of Spain's dominions in South America. That put Peru's capital on the dry side of the line. It did not put most of its people there.

In 1940, Peru's census found most of them in the highlands, in the mountains the line runs along. Fewer than three in ten lived in the region the census calls the coast.

Then, census by census, the balance tipped. The coast became the largest of the three regions between the censuses of 1961 and 1972. By the 1993 census, more than half of Peruvians lived there. By 2025, nearly six in ten did. Some went east instead, into the rainforest, whose share of Peruvians more than doubled. Peru's statistics institute put it this way: the population had gone from "predominantly Andean" to "mostly coastal."

In a 1995 study, the same institute pointed to a shortage of farmland in the highlands, and called the coast the main destination of people leaving the Andes. Later, the violence of the 1980s and '90s pushed many more. Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission estimated that about half a million people were displaced, many of them to Lima.

Lima and Callao grew from about 650,000 people in 1940 to more than ten and a half million in 2025, from about one in ten Peruvians to about a third. In 2022, Lima and Callao alone produced about two-fifths of Peru's economic output, by the statistics institute's estimate.

Many newcomers built their own homes at the city's edge. In May 1971, 180 families who had taken over a plot of land were moved by the government to a vast, semi-desert stretch of sand south of the city. That ground became Villa El Salvador. By 1981, about one in four people in Lima lived in informal settlements, which Peruvians call barriadas, by census figures Peru's truth commission cites.

A city that size needs water all year, and its river runs low for seven months of it.

From December to April, the Rímac runs high. From May to November, Peru's ombudsman reports, its natural flow falls to about a quarter of that.

So Lima's water utility stores water from the wet months in lakes and reservoirs high in the Andes, and releases it in the dry ones. By its 2007 figures, more than half of the water Lima stores for the dry season sits on the other side of the line. Those far-side lakes lie nearly 15,000 feet up, in the upper Mantaro basin, which drains toward the Amazon. A weather station there, at Marcapomacocha, sits about 65 miles from downtown Lima in a straight line.

The water travels about 14 miles by canal and tunnel to cross the divide. It comes out on the Pacific side, runs down the Santa Eulalia River into the Rímac, and reaches Lima's main treatment plant. The tunnel was designed to carry nearly twice the Rímac's own natural flow in the dry season.

It was built between 1958 and 1962, and the system has been in service since 1963. Peru's weather service says it was built first to power a hydroelectric plant, and also to firm up the river Lima drinks from. The plant, at Huinco, opened in 1964.

The utility calls the tunnel the only way to bring that stored water across. Rómulo Cárhuaz, a watershed analyst at the utility, said in a 2024 interview that the releases run from May 1 to November 30. The utility regulates 19 lakes and three large reservoirs, he said.

The water makes it across the line. On the hills at the city's edge, many homes are not on the network at all.

In figures reported in March 2026, Peru's water regulator counted more than 700,000 people in Lima and Callao without a connection. In the districts it studied, almost all of those homes bought water from tanker trucks, at about six times what connected homes pay.

In San Juan de Miraflores, in southern Lima, Catalina Naupa, 59, told AFP in March 2025 that her water comes by truck. "There are worms in the bottom of the tank," she said. She washes clothes once a week, or every two weeks, to save water. An official at the utility told the agency it brings about one cubic meter a week to each family in the parts of the district without pipes.

On the city's northern edge, in Puente Piedra, a German magazine visited a cooperative of 42 families without water, sewers or electricity, in January 2024. There, Virginia Martínez Morales, 30, a mother of three, ran a hose from a tank up the hill to her door. After a tanker truck slid down the slope and took three houses with it, drivers stopped going up the steepest streets. Another resident, Tula Tinoco Espinoza, began carrying buckets. Most of the families there, the magazine reported, had come down from the Andean regions in search of better work.

The water Lima keeps on the far side of those mountains has only one way through. In 2025, Peru's ombudsman, citing the utility's own plan, warned that depending on a single tunnel is a risk in a major earthquake. Lima has been planning a second tunnel since the 1990s. In 2026, it still had no construction date.

Lima's tunnel isn't the only one. In the north, a tunnel about 12 miles long carries water from the Amazon side to farmland on the coast.

So why do most Peruvians live on the dry side of that line? Not because that side has the water. First, the valleys: about 5,000 years ago, people built a city above one of them. Then the port: in 1535, the Spanish put their capital near a very good one. Then the people: in the 20th century, the country came down from the mountains, to the coast and to that capital. The water had to be brought to them: by canal in the old valleys, through a tunnel across the Andes since the early 1960s, and at the city's edge, by truck.

Every May 1, the utility starts letting out its high lakes, and the water on the Amazon side crosses the divide toward the Rímac. Peru lives on the dry side of the Andes. From May to November, part of its capital's water comes from the other one.
